claim: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) first generated significant interest in the biological community as a result of its ability to image developing embryos with single-cell resolution, inherent optical sectioning, low phototoxicity and high temporal resolution.
source: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) first generated significant interest in the biological community as a result of its ability to image developing embryos with single-cell resolution, inherent optical sectioning, low phototoxicity and high temporal resolution (Huisken et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Huisken et al., 2004, which provides external scholarly support for this historical statement about LSFM.

claim: LSFM can now routinely image biological systems that range from reconstituted macromolecular complexes to intact organs and organisms.
source: Since then, LSFM has undergone a revolution, and depending on the optical configuration, can now routinely image biological systems that range from reconstituted macromolecular complexes (Keller et al., 2007) to intact organs and organisms (Chakraborty et al., 2019; Voigt et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Keller et al., 2007, Chakraborty et al., 2019, and Voigt et al., 2019, which provide external scholarly evidence for the range of biological systems that can be imaged with LSFM.

claim: LSFM delivers light to only the in-focus portion of the specimen, which substantially decreases the illumination burden on the sample.
source: Unlike other microscope modalities that are used to image three-dimensional specimens (e.g. confocal), LSFM delivers light to only the in-focus portion of the specimen, and therefore substantially decreases the illumination burden on the sample.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about how LSFM works compared to other microscopy modalities.

claim: Light-sheet excitation combines with the million-fold parallelization afforded by modern scientific cameras, permitting massive reductions in illumination intensities without compromising the signal-to-noise ratio.
source: Further, light-sheet excitation combines powerfully with the million-fold parallelization afforded by modern scientific cameras, permitting massive reductions in illumination intensities without compromising the signal-to-noise ratio, which significantly reduces the rate of photobleaching and phototoxicity.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the technical advantages of LSFM.

claim: LSFM enables imaging of biological specimens for 1000's of volumes.
source: Consequently, LSFM enables imaging of biological specimens for 1000's of volumes (Dean et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dean et al., 2017, which provides external scholarly evidence for the long-term imaging capability of LSFM.

claim: The widespread adoption of LSFM remains limited.
source: Despite its advantages over other imaging modalities, its widespread adoption remains limited.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' assessment of the current state of LSFM adoption in the field.

claim: The slow adoption of cutting-edge LSFM systems by commercial entities requires that each lab assemble, align, maintain, and operate their own LSFM instruments.
source: In part, this is due to the slow adoption of cutting-edge LSFM systems by commercial entities, and consequently, the requirement that each lab assemble, align, maintain, operate their own LSFM instruments.
evidence: This is an inference about the reasons for limited adoption of LSFM.

claim: The orthogonal geometry of LSFM systems often sterically occludes standard imaging dishes such as multi-well plates.
source: Sample preparation is an additional problem, as the orthogonal geometry of LSFM systems often sterically occludes standard imaging dishes such as multi-well plates.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the geometric constraints of traditional LSFM systems.

claim: In the highest resolution LSFM systems, the reliance on high-NA water-dipping objectives places the sample in direct contact with non-sterile optical surfaces, which compromises long-term imaging.
source: Furthermore, the highest resolution LSFM systems, the reliance on high-NA water-dipping objectives places the sample in direct contact with non-sterile optical surfaces, which compromises long-term imaging.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical limitations of high-resolution LSFM systems.

claim: Modern LSFM systems often lack modalities that render microscopy routinely useful for non-experts, including sample environmental control, oculars, and hardware-based autofocusing schemes.
source: And these matters are made worse because modern LSFM systems often lack modalities that render microscopy routinely useful for non-experts, including sample environmental control (e.g. CO2, temperature, and humidity), oculars, and hardware-based autofocusing schemes.
evidence: This is an inference about the usability limitations of modern LSFM systems.

claim: Gebhardt et al created a bespoke atomic force microscope cantilever that reflected a light-sheet into the ordinary viewing geometry of an inverted microscope.
source: For example, using the same objective for illumination and detection, Gebhardt et al created a bespoke atomic force microscope cantilever that reflected a light-sheet into the ordinary viewing geometry of an inverted microscope (Gebhardt et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gebhardt et al., 2013, which provides external scholarly evidence for this approach.

claim: Several labs developed specialized microfluidics with micromirrors positioned at 45 degrees.
source: Similarly, several labs developed specialized microfluidics with micromirrors positioned at 45 degrees (Galland et al., 2015; Meddens et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Galland et al., 2015 and Meddens et al., 2016, which provide external scholarly evidence for this approach.

claim: Cantilever and micromirror approaches are only compatible with low-NA illumination, have a limited volumetric imaging capacity, and require that the reflective surface be placed in immediate proximity to the specimen, which drastically limits the field of view.
source: Nonetheless, these approaches are only compatible with low-NA illumination (which reduces resolution and optical sectioning), have a limited volumetric imaging capacity, and require that the reflective surface be placed in immediate proximity to the specimen, which drastically limits the field of view.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of cantilever and micromirror approaches based on their design constraints.

claim: A high-NA oil immersion lens (1.49) was combined with lateral interference tilted excitation.
source: More recently, a high-NA oil immersion lens (1.49) was combined with lateral interference tilted excitation (Fadero et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fadero et al., 2018, which provides external scholarly evidence for this approach.

claim: The system using a high-NA oil immersion lens required specialized imaging chambers, used light-sheets that were several microns thick and tilted relative to the imaged focal plane, and suffered from spherical aberrations.
source: However, this system required specialized imaging chambers, used light-sheets that were several microns thick and tilted relative to the imaged focal plane, and owing to the large refractive index mismatch between the objective immersion media and the specimen, suffered from spherical aberrations, which ultimately impact the resolution and sensitivity of the microscope in a depth-dependent manner (Fadero et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fadero et al., 2018, which provides external scholarly evidence for the limitations of this approach.

claim: Each of these single-objective LSFM systems are incompatible with many experimental designs, including biological workhorses like the 96-well plate and large-scale tissue sections.
source: Thus, each of these systems are incompatible with many experimental designs, including biological workhorses like the 96-well plate and large-scale tissue sections.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical limitations of existing single-objective LSFM systems.

claim: Oblique plane microscopy (OPM) illuminates the sample obliquely and captures the fluorescence with the same objective.
source: Unlike most LSFMs that require the light-sheet to be launched from the side or reflected off of a cantilever or microfluidic device, an OPM illuminates the sample obliquely and captures the fluorescence with the same objective (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about how OPM works, with reference to Figure 1A for visual support.

claim: An OPM can be assembled using a standard inverted or upright microscope geometry and is entirely compatible with traditional forms of sample mounting, environment control, and laser-based auto-focusing.
source: As such, an OPM can be assembled using a standard inverted or upright microscope geometry and is entirely compatible with traditional forms of sample mounting (including multi-well plates), environment control, and laser-based auto-focusing.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of OPM based on its design.

claim: In OPM, the fluorescence captured by the primary objective is relayed in an aberration-free remote focusing format to a secondary objective, which creates a 3D replica of the fluorescent signal at its focus that is then imaged by a tilted tertiary objective onto a camera.
source: In OPM, the fluorescence captured by the primary objective is relayed in an aberration-free remote focusing (Botcherby et al., 2012) format to a secondary objective, which creates a 3D replica of the fluorescent signal at its focus that is then imaged by a tilted tertiary objective onto a camera (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the optical design of OPM, with a citation to Botcherby et al., 2012 for the remote focusing concept and reference to Figure 1B for visual support.

claim: Most oblique plane microscopes have had low optical resolution because the tertiary objective fails to capture all of the high-angle rays that are launched from the secondary objective.
source: To date, most oblique plane microscopes have had low optical resolution because the tertiary objective fails to capture all of the high-angle rays that are launched from the secondary objective (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of previous OPM designs, with reference to Figure 1B for visual support.

claim: An OPM can achieve ~300 nm scale resolution by combining air and water objectives with a coverslip-walled immersion chamber.
source: Nevertheless, it was recently demonstrated that an OPM can achieve ~300 nm scale resolution by combining air and water objectives with a coverslip-walled immersion chamber (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2019, which provides external scholarly evidence for this achievement.

claim: As light rays travel from a low to a high refractive index medium, they are refracted at the coverslip interface toward the tertiary objective in a manner that compresses the optical cone of light, and thereby permits capture of the higher angle rays.
source: Here, as light rays travel from a low to a high refractive index medium (e.g. air and water, respectively), they are refracted at the coverslip interface toward the tertiary objective in a manner that compresses the optical cone of light, and thereby permits capture of the higher angle rays (Yang et al., 2019; Figure 1C and Figure 1–figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2019 and references to Figure 1C and Figure 1–figure supplement 1, which provide visual evidence for this optical principle.

claim: Aligning the coverslip-walled immersion chamber is technically challenging.
source: Nevertheless, aligning this chamber, which requires that the coverslip be placed at the proper distance and angle relative to both the secondary and tertiary objectives, while maintaining a proper water immersion for the tertiary objective, although feasible, is technically challenging.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical difficulties of the immersion chamber approach.

claim: The immersion chamber arrangement was only compatible for secondary objectives with a maximum NA of 0.9, as higher NA objectives would collide with the water chamber.
source: Further, this arrangement was only compatible for secondary objectives with a maximum NA of 0.9, as higher NA objectives would collide with the water chamber.
evidence: This is an inference about the physical constraints of the immersion chamber approach.

claim: The authors built an OPM with a bespoke glass-tipped tertiary objective to improve the resolution, field of view, and usability over previous variants.
source: Here, to mitigate these challenges, we built a high-NA OPM equipped with a recently developed glass-tipped tertiary objective (Millett-Sikking and York, 2019) that eliminates the need for an immersion chamber and further improves instrument performance (Appendix 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Millett-Sikking and York, 2019 for the glass-tipped tertiary objective, and the authors state they built this system.

claim: The OPM presented here provides a unique combination of field of view, resolution, volumetric imaging capacity, and speed compared to other single-objective LSFMs and OPMs.
source: Compared to other single-objective LSFMs and OPMs, we demonstrate that this OPM provides a unique and impressive combination of field of view, resolution, volumetric imaging capacity, and speed.
evidence: This is a claim that will be supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The authors imaged nuclear rupture in melanoma cells as they migrate through tightly confined spaces in a microfluidic device.
source: As proof of principle, we image a number of biological processes that would otherwise be challenging to observe without this unique combination of microscope geometry, speed, resolution, and field of view, including nuclear rupture in melanoma cells as they migrate through tightly confined spaces in a microfluidic device, immunological synapse formation, cleavage furrow ingression in developmental systems, rheological cytosolic flows, optogenetic activation of Rac1, and intact imaging of an complete coronal murine brain slice.
evidence: This is a claim that will be supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The authors imaged immunological synapse formation.
source: As proof of principle, we image a number of biological processes that would otherwise be challenging to observe without this unique combination of microscope geometry, speed, resolution, and field of view, including nuclear rupture in melanoma cells as they migrate through tightly confined spaces in a microfluidic device, immunological synapse formation, cleavage furrow ingression in developmental systems, rheological cytosolic flows, optogenetic activation of Rac1, and intact imaging of an complete coronal murine brain slice.
evidence: This is a claim that will be supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The authors imaged cleavage furrow ingression in developmental systems.
source: As proof of principle, we image a number of biological processes that would otherwise be challenging to observe without this unique combination of microscope geometry, speed, resolution, and field of view, including nuclear rupture in melanoma cells as they migrate through tightly confined spaces in a microfluidic device, immunological synapse formation, cleavage furrow ingression in developmental systems, rheological cytosolic flows, optogenetic activation of Rac1, and intact imaging of an complete coronal murine brain slice.
evidence: This is a claim that will be supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The authors imaged rheological cytosolic flows.
source: As proof of principle, we image a number of biological processes that would otherwise be challenging to observe without this unique combination of microscope geometry, speed, resolution, and field of view, including nuclear rupture in melanoma cells as they migrate through tightly confined spaces in a microfluidic device, immunological synapse formation, cleavage furrow ingression in developmental systems, rheological cytosolic flows, optogenetic activation of Rac1, and intact imaging of an complete coronal murine brain slice.
evidence: This is a claim that will be supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The authors imaged optogenetic activation of Rac1.
source: As proof of principle, we image a number of biological processes that would otherwise be challenging to observe without this unique combination of microscope geometry, speed, resolution, and field of view, including nuclear rupture in melanoma cells as they migrate through tightly confined spaces in a microfluidic device, immunological synapse formation, cleavage furrow ingression in developmental systems, rheological cytosolic flows, optogenetic activation of Rac1, and intact imaging of an complete coronal murine brain slice.
evidence: This is a claim that will be supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The authors imaged an intact complete coronal murine brain slice.
source: As proof of principle, we image a number of biological processes that would otherwise be challenging to observe without this unique combination of microscope geometry, speed, resolution, and field of view, including nuclear rupture in melanoma cells as they migrate through tightly confined spaces in a microfluidic device, immunological synapse formation, cleavage furrow ingression in developmental systems, rheological cytosolic flows, optogenetic activation of Rac1, and intact imaging of an complete coronal murine brain slice.
evidence: This is a claim that will be supported by data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The OPM uses a high-NA primary objective (100X, NA 1.35) with an angular aperture of ~74 degrees.
source: In this design, a high-NA primary objective (100X, NA 1.35) with an angular aperture of ~74 degrees is matched to a secondary air objective (40X, NA 0.95) with a similarly large angular aperture, which relays the fluorescence to a tertiary imaging system that is oriented 30 degrees off-axis (See Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the microscope design built by the authors.

claim: The OPM uses a secondary air objective (40X, NA 0.95) with a similarly large angular aperture.
source: In this design, a high-NA primary objective (100X, NA 1.35) with an angular aperture of ~74 degrees is matched to a secondary air objective (40X, NA 0.95) with a similarly large angular aperture, which relays the fluorescence to a tertiary imaging system that is oriented 30 degrees off-axis (See Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the microscope design built by the authors.

claim: The tertiary imaging system is oriented 30 degrees off-axis.
source: In this design, a high-NA primary objective (100X, NA 1.35) with an angular aperture of ~74 degrees is matched to a secondary air objective (40X, NA 0.95) with a similarly large angular aperture, which relays the fluorescence to a tertiary imaging system that is oriented 30 degrees off-axis (See Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the microscope design built by the authors.

claim: A silicone immersion primary objective was chosen because the refractive index of living cells (~1.40) is closer to silicone (1.40) than water (1.333) or oil (1.52), thus reducing spherical aberrations and improving the overall imaging performance.
source: We chose a silicone immersion primary objective because the refractive index of living cells (~1.40) is closer to silicone (1.40) than water (1.333) or oil (1.52), thus reducing spherical aberrations and improving the overall imaging performance (Phillips et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a design choice made by the authors, with a citation to Phillips et al., 2012 for the rationale.

claim: The optical train was carefully designed to properly map the pupils of the primary and secondary objectives and lenses were selected that maximized the near-diffraction-limited field of view.
source: To achieve aberration- and distortion-free imaging, the optical train was carefully designed to properly map the pupils of the primary and secondary objectives and lenses were selected that maximized the near-diffraction-limited field of view (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a description of the microscope design built by the authors, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for visual support.

claim: The microscope was equipped with a high-speed galvanometer mirror conjugate to both the primary and secondary objective pupils, allowing for rapid light-sheet scanning in sample space, and rapid emission descanning prior to detection with the camera.
source: Inspired by tilt-invariant imaging systems (Kumar et al., 2018; Voleti et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019), the microscope was equipped with a high-speed galvanometer mirror conjugate to both the primary and secondary objective pupils, allowing for rapid light-sheet scanning in sample space, and rapid emission descanning prior to detection with the camera.
evidence: This is a description of the microscope design built by the authors, with citations to Kumar et al., 2018, Voleti et al., 2019, and Yang et al., 2019 for the inspiration.

claim: Because the galvanometer mirror is the only moving part, sources of optical drift are minimized.
source: Because the galvanometer mirror is the only moving part, sources of optical drift are minimized, and only a portion of the camera is necessary to detect the descanned fluorescence (~256×2048), which permits very high imaging rates (~800 planes per second).
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the galvanometer-based design.

claim: Only a portion of the camera is necessary to detect the descanned fluorescence (~256×2048), which permits very high imaging rates (~800 planes per second).
source: Because the galvanometer mirror is the only moving part, sources of optical drift are minimized, and only a portion of the camera is necessary to detect the descanned fluorescence (~256×2048), which permits very high imaging rates (~800 planes per second).
evidence: This is a description of the imaging capabilities of the microscope built by the authors.

claim: The authors developed a versatile laser launch that can be reconfigured in a fully automatic fashion to illuminate the cells with either an oblique light-sheet that is equipped with resonant multi-directional shadow suppression, widefield, or a laser-scanned and near-diffraction-limited beam for localized optogenetic stimulation, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, or photoactivation.
source: Furthermore, for illumination, we developed a versatile laser launch that can be reconfigured in a fully automatic fashion to illuminate the cells with either an oblique light-sheet that is equipped with resonant multi-directional shadow suppression (Huisken and Stainier, 2007), widefield, or a laser-scanned and near-diffraction-limited beam for localized optogenetic stimulation, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching, or photoactivation (See Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplements 3–7).
evidence: This is a description of the illumination system built by the authors, with a citation to Huisken and Stainier, 2007 for the shadow suppression concept and references to Figure 1—figure supplements 3–7 for visual support.

claim: Absorption and spurious reflections resulted in a 59 and 47% decrease in fluorescence transmission for the laser-scanning and stage-scanning variants of the microscope, respectively, at 30-degrees.
source: Owing to the large number of optics, absorption and spurious reflections resulted in a 59 and 47% decrease in fluorescence transmission for the laser-scanning and stage-scanning variants of the microscope, respectively, at 30-degrees.
evidence: This is a measurement of the transmission efficiency of the microscope built by the authors.

claim: Transmission improved only slightly (3%) when the optical system was arranged at 0-degrees.
source: Transmission improved only slightly (3%) when the optical system was arranged at 0-degrees, indicating that the tertiary objective was indeed capable of capturing most of the transmitted light under a 30-degree tilt.
evidence: This is a measurement of the transmission efficiency of the microscope built by the authors.

claim: The entire microscope was built in a standard inverted format with a motorized sample stage, objective and sample heating, and a temperature and CO2-regulated environmental chamber.
source: The entire microscope was built in a standard inverted format with a motorized sample stage, objective and sample heating, and a temperature and CO2-regulated environmental chamber.
evidence: This is a description of the microscope built by the authors.

claim: An obliquely oriented light-sheet is launched from a single objective into the specimen at an angle of 30 degrees, simultaneously illuminating a two-dimensional plane along the X and S axes.
source: An obliquely oriented light-sheet is launched from a single objective into the specimen at an angle of 30 degrees, simultaneously illuminating a two-dimensional plane along the X and S axes.
evidence: This is a description of how the microscope operates.

claim: By scanning the laser in the Y-direction and collecting images at each intermediate XS plane, a three-dimensional volume is acquired.
source: By scanning the laser in the Y-direction and collecting images at each intermediate XS plane, a three-dimensional volume is acquired (Figure 2A,B and C).
evidence: This is a description of how the microscope operates, with reference to Figure 2A, B, and C for visual support.

claim: Computationally shearing places the data into its proper Euclidian context and results in a parallelepiped-shaped image volume.
source: Computationally shearing places these data into its proper Euclidian context and results in a parallelepiped-shaped image volume, which is readily visualized by imaging 100 nm green fluorescent beads embedded in a 1% agarose gel (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a description of the data processing method, with reference to Figure 2D for visual support.

claim: At the highest illumination NA (0.34), the raw axial resolution is 587 ± 18 nm (mean and standard deviation of the Full-Width Half Maximum, FWHM).
source: Here, at the highest illumination NA (0.34), a narrow strip of beads coincident with the illumination beam waist appear sharp. By fitting each bead to a three-dimensional Gaussian function, the raw (e.g. non-deconvolved) axial resolution for these data are 587 ± 18 nm (mean and standard deviation of the Full-Width Half Maximum, FWHM, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a measurement of the axial resolution of the microscope, with reference to Figure 2E for visual support.

claim: As the NA of the illumination decreases, the raw axial resolution reduces to 736 ± 10 nm and 918 ± 12 nm, for NA 0.16 and NA 0.06 illumination beams, respectively.
source: As the NA of the illumination decreases, the length and thickness of the light-sheet grows. While this improves the uniformity of the resolution and contrast throughout the field of view spanned by the XS plane, it ultimately reduces the raw axial resolution to 736 ± 10 nm and 918 ± 12 nm, for NA 0.16 and NA 0.06 illumination beams, respectively (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a measurement of the axial resolution of the microscope at different illumination NAs, with reference to Figure 2D and E for visual support.

claim: For most biological experiments reported here, an illumination NA of 0.16 was used, yielding a Gaussian beam that has a thickness and propagation length of ~1.2 and~37 microns, respectively.
source: For most biological experiments reported here, we used an illumination NA of 0.16, yielding a Gaussian beam that has a thickness and propagation length of ~1.2 and~37 microns, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging parameters used by the authors.

claim: The OPM delivers adequate optical sectioning over the full range of excitation NAs used in this manuscript.
source: Nonetheless, as is evident from the PSF and optical transfer function, the OPM presented here delivers adequate optical sectioning over the full range of excitation NAs used in this manuscript (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a claim about the optical sectioning capability of the microscope, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for visual support.

claim: The maximum imaging depth of the remote focusing system is ~60 microns.
source: Theoretically, the maximum imaging depth of our remote focusing system is ~60 microns, beyond which tiling in the Z-dimension can be performed until one reaches the working distance of the primary objective (300 microns).
evidence: This is a theoretical calculation of the imaging depth of the microscope.

claim: A gradual loss in NA and thus resolution was observed as the tertiary imaging system was adjusted from a 0 to a 30-degree tilt.
source: Of note, the choice of illumination angle is accompanied by tradeoffs in light-sheet thickness, imaging depth, detection efficiency, and resolution (Appendix 2). Indeed, we observed a gradual loss in NA and thus resolution as our tertiary imaging system was adjusted from a 0 to a 30-degree tilt.
evidence: This is a measurement of the resolution of the microscope at different tilt angles.

claim: Unlike single-objective light-sheet systems that use oil immersion objectives, spherical aberrations are not immediately evident.
source: Unlike single-objective light-sheet systems that use oil immersion objectives (Fadero et al., 2018), spherical aberrations are not immediately evident (Figure 2D and E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a comparison of the microscope to other systems, with a citation to Fadero et al., 2018 and references to Figure 2D, E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for visual support.

claim: For an oblique illumination angle of 30 degrees and an excitation NA of 0.16, the raw axial resolution of the OPM is similar to the raw 666 nm axial resolution reported for the most commonly used square illumination mode of lattice light-sheet microscopy.
source: For an oblique illumination angle of 30 degrees and an excitation NA of 0.16, the raw axial resolution of our system is similar to the raw 666 nm axial resolution reported for the most commonly used square illumination mode of lattice light-sheet microscopy (Chang et al., 2020; Valm et al., 2017) or a spinning-disk microscope using the same NA 1.35/100X objective used here (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a comparison of the microscope to other systems, with citations to Chang et al., 2020 and Valm et al., 2017 and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3 for visual support.

claim: For raw data, the resolution was measured as 299 ± 21, 336 ± 16, and 731 ± 21 nm in X, Y, and Z, respectively, throughout a lateral field of view of ~180 x~180 microns.
source: For raw data, we measured a resolution of 299 ± 21, 336 ± 16, and 731 ± 21 nm in X, Y, and Z, respectively, throughout a lateral field of view of ~180 x~180 microns (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a measurement of the resolution of the microscope using 100 nm coverslip-immobilized fluorescent beads, with reference to Figure 2F for visual support.

claim: In the central ~60 x~60 micron portion of the field of view, a slightly improved lateral resolution was observed (284 ± 12 and 328 ± 14 for X and Y, respectively).
source: In the central ~60 x~60 micron portion of the field of view, a slightly improved lateral resolution was observed (284 ± 12 and 328 ± 14 for X and Y, respectively).
evidence: This is a measurement of the resolution of the microscope in the central portion of the field of view.

claim: The resolution was relatively uniform throughout the full ~180 x~180 micron field of view.
source: Nonetheless, the resolution was relatively uniform throughout the full ~180 x~180 micron field of view (e.g. the footprint of the imaging volume in X and Y), which importantly is 2.6x, 3.8x, 37.9x, and 268x larger than reported for lattice light-sheet microscopy (Chen et al., 2014), eSPIM (Yang et al., 2019), micromirror (Galland et al., 2015; Meddens et al., 2016), and atomic force microscopy (AFM) cantilever-based methods (Gebhardt et al., 2013), respectively (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a comparison of the field of view of the microscope to other systems, with citations to Chen et al., 2014, Yang et al., 2019, Galland et al., 2015, Meddens et al., 2016, and Gebhardt et al., 2013 and reference to Figure 2G for visual support.

claim: The lateral extent of the imaging field (e.g. the X-dimension) in a laser-scanning format is ~2.6 x larger than those reported for eSPIM.
source: Nonetheless, through careful optical design, the lateral extent of our imaging field (e.g. the X- dimension) in a laser-scanning format is ~2.6 x larger than those reported for eSPIM (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a comparison of the field of view of the microscope to eSPIM, with a citation to Yang et al., 2019.

claim: Decorrelation analysis for the 180 × 180 micron field of view resulted in an aggregate raw lateral resolution (e.g. the average of both the X and Y dimensions) of 325 ± 25 nm (mean and standard deviation).
source: Decorrelation analysis for the 180 × 180 micron field of view resulted in an aggregate raw lateral resolution (e.g. the average of both the X and Y dimensions) of 325 ± 25 nm (mean and standard deviation, Figure 2—figure supplement 4), which is in good agreement with our FWHM measurements.
evidence: This is a measurement of the resolution of the microscope using image decorrelation analysis, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 4 for visual support.

claim: 20 iterations of Richardson-Lucy deconvolution yielded resolutions of 203 ± 24, 209 ± 33, and 523 ± 60 nm in X, Y, and Z, respectively.
source: Here, 20 iterations of Richardson-Lucy deconvolution yielded resolutions of 203 ± 24, 209 ± 33, and 523 ± 60 nm in X, Y, and Z, respectively, and representative point spread functions for both raw and deconvolved data are shown in Figure 2H.
evidence: This is a measurement of the resolution of the microscope after deconvolution, with reference to Figure 2H for visual support.

claim: Microscope performance remained robust even when imaging beyond the nominal focal plane of the primary objective.
source: Furthermore, microscope performance remained robust even when imaging beyond the nominal focal plane of the primary objective (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a claim about the robustness of the microscope, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 5 for visual support.

claim: Using Fourier Ring Correlation analysis, an aggregate lateral resolution of 343 ± 12 and 220 ± 23 nm was measured for raw and deconvolved GEMs, respectively.
source: Using Fourier Ring Correlation analysis, which evaluates the spatial frequency-dependent signal-to-noise for a pair of images, we measured an aggregate lateral resolution of 343 ± 12 and 220 ± 23 nm, for raw and deconvolved GEMs, respectively (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is a measurement of the resolution of the microscope using GEMs and Fourier Ring Correlation analysis, with reference to Figure 2J for visual support.

claim: The raw lateral resolution for lattice light-sheet microscopy for a GFP-like fluorophore is 312 nm.
source: By comparison, the raw lateral resolution for lattice light-sheet microscopy for a GFP-like fluorophore is 312 nm (Valm et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparison of the microscope to lattice light-sheet microscopy, with a citation to Valm et al., 2017.

claim: When compared to other single-objective LSFMs, OPMs, and even lattice light-sheet microscopy, the OPM presented here achieves a unique combination of resolution, field of view, and rapid imaging.
source: Thus, when compared to other single-objective LSFMs, OPMs, and even lattice light-sheet microscopy, the OPM presented here achieves a unique combination of resolution, field of view, and rapid imaging.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the performance of the microscope compared to other systems.

claim: The authors imaged the endoplasmic reticulum in U2OS osteosarcoma cells.
source: To evaluate microscope performance on biological specimens, we first imaged the endoplasmic reticulum in U2OS osteosarcoma cells (Figure 3A, and Video 1).
evidence: This is a description of a biological imaging experiment performed by the authors, with reference to Figure 3A and Video 1 for visual support.

claim: Endoplasmic reticulum tubules were highly dynamic.
source: Endoplasmic reticulum tubules were highly dynamic, and unlike methods that rely on imaging slightly out of a total internal reflection geometry (Li et al., 2015), could be imaged with high-resolution throughout the entire cell volume.
evidence: This is an observation from the biological imaging experiment, with a citation to Li et al., 2015 for comparison.

claim: The authors imaged vimentin in retinal pigment epithelial cells.

claim: Vimentin appeared as moderately dynamic filamentous structures that extended from the perinuclear region to the cell periphery.

claim: Endocytosis could be observed through time, with individual endocytic pits appearing as point-like structures that initialized on the plasma membrane, locally diffused, and then disappeared upon scission and release into the cytosol.
source: Endocytosis could be observed through time, with individual endocytic pits appearing as point-like structures that initialized on the plasma membrane, locally diffused, and then disappeared upon scission and release into the cytosol.

claim: The authors imaged MV3 melanoma cells tagged with a membrane marker.

claim: Short lived filopodial buckling events were observed in MV3 melanoma cells.

claim: Natural Killer (NK) cells are one of the main components of the innate immune system and are able to directly recognize and destroy virally infected or oncogenically transformed cells via the formation of a multi-purpose interface called the immunological synapse with their target.
source: Natural Killer (NK) cells are one of the main components of the innate immune system and are able to directly recognize and destroy virally infected or oncogenically transformed cells via the formation of a multi-purpose interface called the immunological synapse with their target (Mace et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about NK cells, with a citation to Mace et al., 2014.

claim: An early landmark of the immunological synapse is the establishment of a complex actin scaffold (on the effector side) which formation and dynamism are known to be critical to ensure the productive outcome of the cytotoxic process.
source: An early landmark of this structure is the establishment of a complex actin scaffold (on the effector side) which formation (Mace and Orange, 2014) and dynamism (Carisey et al., 2018) are known to be critical to ensure the productive outcome of the cytotoxic process.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the immunological synapse, with citations to Mace and Orange, 2014 and Carisey et al., 2018.

claim: The contribution of the target cell in the establishment and maintenance of the immunological synapse, and the interplay between the plasma membranes of the two cells remains poorly understood.
source: By contrast, the contribution of the target cell in the establishment and maintenance of this unique structure, and the interplay between the plasma membranes of the two cells remains poorly understood, in part because most work has been performed on ligand-coated surfaces (Brown et al., 2011; Carisey et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference about the current state of knowledge in the field, with citations to Brown et al., 2011 and Carisey et al., 2018.

claim: The authors imaged the formation of the cytolytic immunological synapse between a population of NK cells expressing a reporter for filamentous actin and myelogenous leukemia cancer cells expressing a fluorescent marker highlighting their plasma membrane.
source: Here, we imaged the formation of the cytolytic immunological synapse between a population of NK cells expressing a reporter for filamentous actin and myelogenous leukemia cancer cells expressing a fluorescent marker highlighting their plasma membrane (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a description of a biological imaging experiment performed by the authors, with reference to Figure 4A for visual support.

claim: Upon engaging with the cancer cell, the NK cell formed an immunological synapse with rapid actin accumulation in the plane of the immune synapse followed by the establishment of an actin retrograde flow along the cell axis.
source: Upon engaging with the cancer cell, the NK cell formed an immunological synapse with rapid actin accumulation in the plane of the immune synapse followed by the establishment of an actin retrograde flow along the cell axis in a similar fashion to what has been observed in T cells (Chen et al., 2014; Ritter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation from the biological imaging experiment, with citations to Chen et al., 2014 and Ritter et al., 2015 for comparison.

claim: Long tethers of membrane were pulled from the target cell synchronously with the actin retrograde flow.
source: Interestingly, long tethers of membrane were pulled from the target cell synchronously with the actin retrograde flow (Figure 4B,C and D, Video 6).
evidence: This is an observation from the biological imaging experiment, with reference to Figure 4B, C, D, and Video 6 for visual support.

claim: The observation of membrane tethers could be a direct visualization of the first stage of trogocytosis.
source: This could be a direct visualization of the first stage of trogocytosis, an important consequence of mechanotransduction at the immunological synapse that contributes to hypo-responsiveness in cytotoxic cells (Miner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observation, with a citation to Miner et al., 2015.

claim: Recent work performed on cytolytic T cells emphasized the crucial role of tension transmitted through the ligand-receptor axis on the organization of the underlying actin cytoskeleton.
source: Indeed, recent work performed on cytolytic T cells emphasized the crucial role of tension transmitted through the ligand-receptor axis on the organization of the underlying actin cytoskeleton (Kumari et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement of recent findings in the field, with a citation to Kumari et al., 2020.

claim: Cells migrating through 3D microenvironments such as dense stromal tissues must navigate through tight pores between matrix fibers and are thus rate-limited by the cross-sectional diameter of their nucleus.
source: Cells migrating through 3D microenvironments such as dense stromal tissues must navigate through tight pores between matrix fibers and are thus rate-limited by the cross-sectional diameter of their nucleus (Wolf et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about cell migration, with a citation to Wolf et al., 2013.

claim: During 3D migration cells can tolerate and repair nuclear constriction events that cause nuclear herniation, rupture and DNA damage.
source: For example, we now know that during 3D migration cells can tolerate and repair nuclear constriction events that cause nuclear herniation, rupture and DNA damage (Denais et al., 2016; Raab et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of recent findings in the field, with citations to Denais et al., 2016 and Raab et al., 2016.

claim: Microfluidic devices provide an accurate and reproducible model of nuclear constriction whereby cells can be subjected to precisely-defined mechanical constrictions with unique sizes and shapes that serve to recapitulate the biological microenvironment.
source: In contrast, microfluidic devices provide an accurate and reproducible model of this phenomenon whereby cells can be subjected to precisely-defined mechanical constrictions with unique sizes and shapes that serve to recapitulate the biological microenvironment (Garcia-Arcos et al., 2019; Raab et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about microfluidic devices, with citations to Garcia-Arcos et al., 2019 and Raab et al., 2016.

claim: The glass-polydimethylsiloxane sandwich geometry of microfluidic devices is not compatible with traditional LSFMs that use water-dipping objectives and an orthogonal illumination and detection geometry.
source: While light-sheet microscopy is an attractive alternative, the glass-polydimethylsiloxane sandwich geometry of microfluidic devices is not compatible with traditional LSFMs that use water-dipping objectives and an orthogonal illumination and detection geometry, let alone cantilever- or micromirror-based methods.
evidence: This is an inference about the incompatibility of microfluidic devices with traditional LSFM systems.

claim: Using the OPM, the authors were able to volumetrically image nuclear positioning and microtubule dynamics as cells navigated mechanical constrictions.
source: Here, using our OPM, we were able to circumvent this and volumetrically image nuclear positioning and microtubule dynamics as cells navigated mechanical constrictions (Figure 5A, Video 7).
evidence: This is a description of a biological imaging experiment performed by the authors, with reference to Figure 5A and Video 7 for visual support.

claim: The microfluidic device consists of ~4 microns tall large and small circular posts with constriction junctions between large and small posts of 2.5 microns and two microns, respectively.
source: Here, the microfluidic device consists of ~4 microns tall large and small circular posts with constriction junctions between large and small posts of 2.5 microns and two microns, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a description of the microfluidic device used in the experiment, with reference to Figure 5B for visual support.

claim: When cells were allowed to migrate within the microchannels, cells generated long, microtubule-rich protrusions, and migrated in a polarized manner.
source: When cells were allowed to migrate within these microchannels, cells generated long, microtubule-rich protrusions, and migrated in a polarized manner.
evidence: This is an observation from the biological imaging experiment.

claim: The nucleus was visibly compressed when viewed in the axial direction.
source: The nucleus was visibly compressed when viewed in the axial direction (Figure 5C) and appeared to be surrounded by microtubules on both the apical and basal surfaces of the nucleus (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is an observation from the biological imaging experiment, with reference to Figure 5C, D, and E for visual support.

claim: As cells squeezed through the microfluidic device, they adopted particularly elongated morphologies (~80 microns).
source: Importantly, as these cells squeezed through the microfluidic device, they adopted particularly elongated morphologies (~80 microns) that otherwise would be challenging to observe if it were not for the large field of view of our OPM.
evidence: This is an observation from the biological imaging experiment.

claim: Because the OPM adopts a galvanometer-based scan-descan optical geometry, camera framerate-limited imaging is possible.
source: Nevertheless, because the OPM described here adopts a galvanometer-based scan-descan optical geometry, camera framerate-limited imaging is possible (Kumar et al., 2018; Voleti et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference about the imaging speed of the microscope, with citations to Kumar et al., 2018, Voleti et al., 2019, and Yang et al., 2019.

claim: The authors imaged rat primary cardiomyocytes using the small-molecule calcium sensor Fluo-3 at a volumetric image acquisition rate of 10.4 Hz.
source: For the former, we used the small-molecule calcium sensor Fluo-3, and imaged rat primary cardiomyocytes at a volumetric image acquisition rate of 10.4 Hz (Figure 6A, Video 8).
evidence: This is a description of a biological imaging experiment performed by the authors, with reference to Figure 6A and Video 8 for visual support.

claim: Imaging was sufficiently fast to observe calcium translocation during spontaneous cardiomyocyte contraction.
source: Here, imaging was sufficiently fast to observe calcium translocation during spontaneous cardiomyocyte contraction.
evidence: This is an observation from the biological imaging experiment.

claim: Such imaging can improve the understanding of single-cell calcium waves which is important for cardiac physiology and disease.
source: Such imaging can improve the understanding of single-cell calcium waves which is important for cardiac physiology and disease (Gilbert et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the imaging, with a citation to Gilbert et al., 2020.

claim: The authors imaged genetically encoded multimeric nanoparticles in live cells at a volumetric image acquisition rate of 13.7 Hz.
source: Likewise, we also evaluated the rheological properties of the cytoplasm by imaging in live cells genetically encoded multimeric nanoparticles. These nanoparticles appeared as near-diffraction-limited puncta that rapidly diffused and thus served as inert cytoplasmic tracers, and which we were able to image and track (Jaqaman et al., 2008) over 100 time points at a volumetric image acquisition rate of 13.7 Hz (Figure 6B, Video 9).
evidence: This is a description of a biological imaging experiment performed by the authors, with a citation to Jaqaman et al., 2008 for the tracking method and reference to Figure 6B and Video 9 for visual support.

claim: Tracking of nanoparticles can help understand how diffusion varies for different morphological domains, as well as how phenotypic changes alter cellular mechanics.

evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the imaging, with citations to Delarue et al., 2018 and Hannezo and Heisenberg, 2019.

claim: Rac1 drives changes in cell shape and migration.
source: In addition to its effects on proliferation and survival (Mohan et al., 2019), Rac1 also drives changes in cell shape and migration.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Rac1, with a citation to Mohan et al., 2019.

source: By analyzing the protrusion dynamics in multiple cells (See Materials and methods), those expressing PA-Rac1 (N = 7) showed statistically significant increases in protrusion speed (p=0.04) and protrusion duration (p=0.02), but not the frequency of protrusion-retraction dynamics, upon photoactivation.

claim: Optically stimulated control cells (N = 6) did not show any significant change in protrusion speed, duration, or frequency in response to photoactivation.
source: Importantly, optically stimulated control cells (N = 6) did not show any significant change in protrusion speed, duration, or frequency in response to photoactivation (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a quantitative analysis of the biological imaging experiment, with reference to Figure 7E for visual support.

claim: Neurons rapidly transduce action potentials across large spatial distances via their axonal or dendritic arbors.
source: Neurons rapidly transduce action potentials across large spatial distances via their axonal or dendritic arbors, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about neurons.

source: However, many neuronal features, including synaptic boutons, are sub-micron in scale.

claim: Many developmental programs, including ventral furrow ingression in Drosophila, are inherently three-dimensional as cells are rapidly internalized on the timescale of a few minutes along the anteroposterior axis of the embryo which spans ~230 microns.
source: Indeed, many developmental programs, including ventral furrow ingression in Drosophila, are inherently three-dimensional as cells are rapidly internalized on the timescale of a few minutes along the anteroposterior axis of the embryo which spans ~230 microns.

source: This global cell movement causes the tissue to elongate, which is immediately followed by rapid cellular rounding and mitotic events.

source: Indeed, by combining scan optimized equipment with fully automated fluidic handling, it is possible to image ~1 cm2 of a thin tissue in less than 45 min per color and perform biochemistry, such as sequential multiplexed labeling.

claim: The authors imaged an entire 30-micron thick slice of coronal mouse brain tissue labeled with the nuclear marker DAPI.

claim: Within the mouse brain tissue data, even small features like nucleoli are clearly resolved from both lateral and axial viewing perspectives throughout the entire ~6×8 mm tissue slice.
source: Within these data, even small features like nucleoli are clearly resolved from both lateral and axial viewing perspectives throughout the entire ~6×8 mm tissue slice (Figure 9B and C).
evidence: This is an observation from the biological imaging experiment, with reference to Figure 9B and C for visual support.

claim: The authors imaged a ~ 4×14 mm slice of 12-micron thick human lung tissue labeled for nuclei, angiotension-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) mRNA, and surfactant protein C (SFTPC) protein.
source: Likewise, we also imaged a ~ 4×14 mm slice of 12-micron thick human lung tissue labeled for nuclei, angiotension-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) mRNA, and surfactant protein C (SFTPC) protein (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is a description of a biological imaging experiment performed by the authors, with reference to Figure 9D for visual support.

claim: Characteristic histological features, including bronchiole, alveoli and vasculature, are readily visible in the human lung tissue.
source: Here, characteristic histological features, including bronchiole, alveoli and vasculature, are readily visible, albeit with molecular contrast and sub-cellular resolution (Figure 9E,F and G, and Video 16).
evidence: This is an observation from the biological imaging experiment, with reference to Figure 9E, F, G, and Video 16 for visual support.

claim: Quantification of molecular expression within the human lung tissue section provides spatial information on ~20,000 cells.
source: Quantification of molecular expression within this tissue section provides spatial information on ~20,000 cells, and verifies our previous limited quantification of ACE2 expression in alveolar epithelial type II cells using confocal microscopy (Muus and Luecken, 2020).

claim: The lateral dimensions of the human lung specimen were 8- and 1.5-fold larger than those of the biggest sample imaged with lattice light-sheet microscopy.
source: Indeed, because we were not sterically restricted by the orthogonal illumination and detection geometry (Figure 9—figure supplement 1), the lateral dimensions of this human lung specimen were 8- and 1.5-fold larger than those of the biggest sample imaged with lattice light-sheet microscopy (Gao et al., 2019).

claim: In the third dimension, lattice light-sheet microscopy has in principle a 6.7x larger reach (2 mm working distance of the typically employed NA 1.1/25X detection objective compared to 300 microns working distance of the OPM primary objective).
source: However, in the third dimension, lattice light-sheet microscopy has in principle a 6.7x larger reach (2 mm working distance of the typically employed NA 1.1/25X detection objective compared to 300 microns working distance of our primary objective).
evidence: This is a comparison of the imaging depth of the microscope to lattice light-sheet microscopy.

claim: In practice, optical aberrations limit high-resolution light-sheet microscopy to depths of a few hundreds of microns, even for highly transparent samples.
source: In practice, optical aberrations limit high-resolution light-sheet microscopy to depths of a few hundreds of microns, even for highly transparent samples.
evidence: This is an inference about the practical limitations of high-resolution light-sheet microscopy.

claim: The OPM approach is fully compatible with automated fluid exchange, which is increasingly important for projects like the Human Cell Atlas that necessitate iterative imaging approaches for spatial -omics of RNAs and proteins at the single-cell level throughout entire tissues.
source: Furthermore, our approach is fully compatible with automated fluid exchange, which is increasingly important for projects like the Human Cell Atlas that necessitate iterative imaging approaches for spatial -omics of RNAs and proteins at the single-cell level throughout entire tissues (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a claim about the compatibility of the microscope with automated fluid exchange, with a citation to Chen et al., 2015.

claim: High-resolution light-sheet microscopy has yet to be widely adopted in biological laboratories and core facilities owing to routine problems with sample drift, contamination, and lack of user friendliness.
source: High-resolution light-sheet microscopy has yet to be widely adopted in biological laboratories and core facilities owing to routine problems with sample drift, contamination, and lack of user friendliness.
evidence: This is an inference about the current state of adoption of high-resolution light-sheet microscopy.

claim: The OPM overcomes the challenges of sample drift, contamination, and lack of user friendliness, and combines the ease of traditional sample mounting, environment maintenance, and multi-position stage control with the gentle, subcellular imaging afforded by selective plane illumination.
source: Here, we show that an OPM with customized optics overcomes these challenges, and combines the ease of traditional sample mounting, environment maintenance, and multi-position stage control with the gentle, subcellular imaging afforded by selective plane illumination.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the advantages of the OPM.

claim: Cells were easily identified in a traditional epi-fluorescence format prior to volumetric imaging in the light-sheet mode.
source: For example, cells were easily identified in a traditional epi-fluorescence format prior to volumetric imaging in the light-sheet mode, the focus was maintained with readily available hardware solutions, and the environment remained sterile with CO2, humidity, and temperature control.
evidence: This is a description of the ease of use of the microscope.

claim: The OPM delivers spatial resolution that is on par with lattice light-sheet microscopy in its most commonly used square lattice illumination mode, albeit with a larger field of view and a volumetric imaging speed that is only limited by the maximum camera framerate and the emitted fluorescence photon flux.
source: In addition to its ease of use, the OPM described here delivers spatial resolution that is on par with lattice light-sheet microscopy in its most commonly used square lattice illumination mode (Chen et al., 2014), albeit with a larger field of view and a volumetric imaging speed that is only limited by the maximum camera framerate and the emitted fluorescence photon flux.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the performance of the OPM compared to lattice light-sheet microscopy, with a citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: Unlike state-of-the-art multiview LSFM techniques that achieve a better axial resolution after image fusion and deconvolution, only a single imaging perspective is needed with the OPM.
source: And unlike state-of-the-art multiview LSFM techniques that achieve a better axial resolution after image fusion and deconvolution, only a single imaging perspective is needed (Guo et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison of the OPM to multiview LSFM techniques, with citations to Guo et al., 2020 and Wu et al., 2013.

claim: Higher axial resolution can be achieved with Axially Swept Light-Sheet Microscopy or the less commonly used hexagonal and structured illumination modes of lattice light-sheet microscopy.
source: Higher axial resolution can be achieved with Axially Swept Light-Sheet Microscopy (Dean et al., 2015) or the less commonly used hexagonal and structured illumination modes of lattice light-sheet microscopy.
evidence: This is a statement about alternative methods for achieving higher axial resolution, with a citation to Dean et al., 2015.

claim: Axially Swept Light-Sheet Microscopy and the hexagonal and structured illumination modes of lattice light-sheet microscopy require a separate illumination objective, which introduces steric limitations, and are accompanied by additional drawbacks.
source: However, this requires a separate illumination objective, which introduces steric limitations, and is accompanied by additional drawbacks that include a shorter effective exposure time in Axially Swept Light-Sheet Microscopy, increased amounts of out-of-focus blur for hexagonal lattices, or the acquisition of five images per plane for structured illumination.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of alternative methods for achieving higher axial resolution.

claim: Previous generations of OPM provided only moderate spatial resolution or a limited field of view.
source: This is in stark contrast to previous generations of OPM (Bouchard et al., 2015; Dunsby, 2008; Kumar et al., 2011), which provided only moderate spatial resolution or a limited field of view.
evidence: This is a comparison of the OPM to previous generations of OPM, with citations to Bouchard et al., 2015, Dunsby, 2008, and Kumar et al., 2011.

claim: The revolution in OPM performance was triggered by the insight that one could combine a high-NA (~0.9) air secondary objective with a high-NA (~1.0) water-immersion tertiary objective.
source: This revolution in OPM performance was triggered by the insight that one could combine a high-NA (~0.9) air secondary objective with a high-NA (~1.0) water-immersion tertiary objective (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the key insight that led to improved OPM performance, with a citation to Yang et al., 2019.

claim: In the system combining a high-NA air secondary objective with a high-NA water-immersion tertiary objective, the refractive index interface between the two objectives compresses and refracts the optical cone of light toward the tertiary objective and improves both sensitivity and resolution of the entire imaging system.
source: In such a system, the refractive index interface between the two objectives compresses and refracts the optical cone of light toward the tertiary objective and improves both sensitivity and resolution of the entire imaging system.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about the optical principle behind the improved OPM performance.

claim: The authors take the concept of combining a high-NA air secondary objective with a high-NA water-immersion tertiary objective to its extreme with an optimized optical train, and replace the tertiary objective (and its water chamber and coverslip) with a solid immersion objective that eases alignment and more efficiently compresses and refracts the optical cone of light.
source: In this work, we take this concept to its extreme with an optimized optical train, and we replace the tertiary objective (and its water chamber and coverslip) with a solid immersion objective that eases alignment and more efficiently compresses and refracts the optical cone of light (Millett-Sikking and York, 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the key innovation of the OPM presented in this work, with a citation to Millett-Sikking and York, 2019.

claim: The authors characterize the performance of the OPM and demonstrate that it has a lateral and axial resolving power that is similar to or better than many LSFM systems.
source: We characterize the performance of this system and demonstrate that it has a lateral and axial resolving power that is similar to or better than many LSFM systems.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the performance of the OPM.

claim: The theoretical NA of 1.28 would in principle allow even higher spatial resolution.
source: We note that the theoretical NA of 1.28 would in principle allow even higher spatial resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the theoretical potential of the microscope.

claim: When using a zero-tilt angle for the tertiary objective, the system routinely delivered 270 nm scale raw lateral resolution across its field of view.
source: Indeed, when using a zero-tilt angle for the tertiary objective, the system routinely delivered 270 nm scale raw lateral resolution across its field of view.
evidence: This is a measurement of the resolution of the microscope at zero-tilt angle.

claim: With reduced tilt angles, even higher resolution than demonstrated in this work should be possible.
source: This indicates that with reduced tilt angles, even higher resolution as demonstrated here should be possible.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential for even higher resolution.

claim: The volumetric image acquisition rate is not limited by piezoelectric scanning of either the sample or the objective, but rather a high-speed galvanometric mirror, so very high temporal resolution is possible.
source: As the volumetric image acquisition rate is not limited by piezoelectric scanning of either the sample or the objective, but rather a high-speed galvanometric mirror, very high temporal resolution is possible.
evidence: This is an inference about the imaging speed of the microscope.

claim: The authors demonstrated volumetric subcellular imaging at rates of 10 Hz, which permitted tracking of intracellular flows and calcium propagation.
source: Here, we demonstrated volumetric subcellular imaging at rates of 10 Hz, which permitted tracking of intracellular flows and calcium propagation.
evidence: This is a summary of the high-speed imaging experiments performed by the authors.

claim: The authors performed imaging in a microfluidic channel and the reproducible subcellular optogenetic activation of Rac1.
source: To demonstrate its utility, we performed a variety of imaging tasks that would be hard or impossible to perform on a traditional LSFM, including imaging in a microfluidic channel and the reproducible subcellular optogenetic activation of Rac1.
evidence: This is a summary of the imaging experiments performed by the authors.

claim: The stage-scanning variant of the OPM permits applications that would otherwise not be feasible with comparable high-resolution light-sheet platforms.
source: Indeed, as shown by imaging cm-scale tissue slices, the stage-scanning variant of this OPM also permits applications that would otherwise not be feasible with comparable high-resolution light-sheet platforms.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the capabilities of the stage-scanning variant of the microscope.

claim: The OPM could displace laser-scanning and spinning-disk confocal microscopes as the workhorse of cell biology in both individual labs and user facilities.
source: As such, we believe that this OPM could displace laser-scanning and spinning-disk confocal microscopes as the workhorse of cell biology in both individual labs and user facilities.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the OPM.

claim: The OPM design allows integration into existing epi-fluorescence frameworks, which decreases the cost of building such an instrument.
source: Importantly, its design allows integration into existing epi-fluorescence frameworks, which decreases the cost of building such an instrument.
evidence: This is an inference about the cost-effectiveness of the OPM.

claim: The OPM combines spatial resolution of a spinning-disk microscope with high volumetric acquisition speed and low phototoxicity afforded by LSFM.
source: Furthermore, it combines spatial resolution of a spinning-disk microscope (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) with high volumetric acquisition speed and low phototoxicity afforded by LSFM.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the advantages of the OPM, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3 for visual support.

claim: The OPM provides comparable spatial resolution to leading light-sheet technologies, including the square illumination mode of lattice light-sheet microscopy, but with simpler sample handling, maintenance of a sterile environment, the ability to perform simultaneous multicolor imaging, and an essentially unlimited field of view in a sample scanning format.
source: It provides comparable spatial resolution to leading light-sheet technologies, including the square illumination mode of lattice light-sheet microscopy, but with simpler sample handling, maintenance of a sterile environment, the ability to perform simultaneous multicolor imaging (Chang et al., 2019), and an essentially unlimited field of view in a sample scanning format.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the advantages of the OPM compared to lattice light-sheet microscopy, with a citation to Chang et al., 2019.

claim: The principle drawback that is inherent to OPM systems is the reduced collection efficiency, which necessarily results from the large number of optics necessary to reorient the fluorescence emission.
source: The principle drawback that is inherent to OPM systems is the reduced collection efficiency, which necessarily results from the large number of optics necessary to reorient the fluorescence emission (Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of OPM systems, with a citation to Kim et al., 2019.

claim: The losses in collection efficiency are in part offset by the higher overall NA of the OPM system relative to other light-sheet microscopes.
source: While these losses are non-negligible, they are in part offset by the higher overall NA of our OPM system relative to other light-sheet microscopes (Appendix 3), For example, in the absence of aberrations, and assuming a lower bound for the overall NA of 1.2 to collect at best ~1.35 and~2.56 times more photons than a NA 1.1 or NA 0.8 objective, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference about the advantages of the higher NA of the OPM system.

claim: For a given laser power, the OPM achieves image contrast and rates of photobleaching comparable to lattice light-sheet microscopy.
source: Consequently, for a given laser power, we achieve image contrast and rates of photobleaching comparable to lattice light-sheet microscopy (Figure 9—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a comparison of the OPM to lattice light-sheet microscopy, with reference to Figure 9—figure supplement 2 for visual support.

claim: Many different variants of OPMs that operate across a range of NAs (1.0–1.35) and magnifications (20 - 100X) have already been designed and numerically evaluated.
source: And lastly, we reported only on the highest resolution OPM variant that incorporates the bespoke glass-tipped tertiary objective. Indeed, many different variants of OPMs that operate across a range of NAs (1.0–1.35) and magnifications (20 - 100X) have already been designed and numerically evaluated.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential for other variants of OPM.

claim: The OPM presented here is the opening prelude to what may be the next generation of user-friendly, and broadly accessible LSFMs.
source: Thus, we consider this the opening prelude to what may be the next generation of user-friendly, and broadly accessible LSFMs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of the OPM.
